chapter: Arranging, Fletcher Henderson and Lucky Millinder
title: Copying for Fletcher Henderson and learning voicing
summary: Before Hampton he copied music for Fletcher Henderson, who taught him in days how to voice for orchestra; Thompson dislikes the mechanical Schillinger system.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Because I finally put all this knowledge together in my writing that I had picked up, and I finally learned how to write, and while I'm saying this, out I forgot all about the
time before I left with Lionel Hampton that I had spent as a copyist for Fletcher Henderson, the famous arranger who wrote for Benny Goodman. You know?

I copied music for Benny Goodman when he was writing -- for Fletcher Henderson when he was writing for Benny Goodman. He was living in the Dunbar Hotel, and he is the one that showed me in about two or three days what I'd been trying to learn in four or five years. How to voice properly for orchestration. I had tried to learn by listening, I had listened to Count Basie's band, all these other writers who had this -- they had different styles, and it was about this time they came out with the famous Schillinger system of writing, which I had actually been using all the time, only I hadn't been doing it mathematically. The Schillinger has to do with mathematics of where the note is supposed to be. It's very mechanical. I don't like it myself, personally. You know, it has no feeling to it, it's all mechanical.
You know, in other words you know that this note is supposed to be in the chord --
And you know it's supposed to be played at a certain time, if that's a chord there, you know.
Like one, two, three, four, six, and
eight, and you know. But Fletcher Henderson is one that taught me.
When you say you learned from Smack, I'm interested to know did Smack actually give you a little help or did you pick it up right out of what you were copying there?
